relationships.sentence: Parent of nearly everything on the map
relationships.other: Nearly everything else on the map
relationships.claim: Claims to be the parent (source) of most later movements.

relationships.sentence: Justin, who told his imperial interrogator that he taught above a public bathhouse in Rome, wrote down the earliest record of what their Sunday actually looked like—the reading of the memoirs, the common loaf and cup, and the collection gathered for orphans, widows, and travelers.
relationships.other_id_note: Justin is named in both entries; this is a shared figure rather than a formal link.
relationships.claim: Justin, a Greek apologist, wrote the earliest record of this movement's Sunday worship (shared figure).

relationships.sentence: Around 112 CE, the governor Pliny the Younger wrote to the emperor Trajan describing an investigation: believers who had recanted told him, under threat of ordinary punishment, that these communities met before dawn to sing a hymn to Christ 'as God,' bound themselves by oath against theft and adultery, then met again later for a meal they called 'common yet harmless.'
relationships.other: Pliny the Younger and the Roman imperial government
relationships.other_id_note: State actor, not a movement.
relationships.claim: Roman governor Pliny investigated these communities and questioned their women officers (outside state attack and record).

relationships.sentence: In the decades after the apostles died, these house churches held together with no fixed hierarchy and no finished New Testament - Ignatius wrote seven letters while under armed guard on his way to execution, and Rome wrote at length to settle a quarrel in Corinth.
relationships.other_id_note: Roman church of c. 96 CE has no census entry; roman-church-third-century covers c. 200-268 only.
relationships.claim: The Roman church corresponded with Corinth to settle a quarrel (correspondence).

relationships.sentence: Almost every Christian tradition descends from these early gatherings.
relationships.claim: Claims later Christian traditions descend from this movement.

relationships.sentence: Overlaps post-apostolic-house-church in era and largely in people - Justin taught at Rome - but is a different thing: that entry is the church's internal life, this is the same Christians turned outward, addressing emperors and an educated public that despised them.
relationships.claim: Overlaps in era and people (Justin); a different thing - the same Christians turned outward.

relationships.sentence: The charges were always roughly the same - that Christians were atheists because they had no images, cannibals because of what they said about eating a body, and disloyal because they would not sacrifice - and the answers were too.
relationships.other: Pagan critics (charges of atheism, cannibalism, disloyalty)
relationships.other_id_note: Named opponents are pagan critics, not a movement.
relationships.claim: Argued against pagan charges against Christians (atheism, cannibalism, disloyalty).

relationships.sentence: What made the enterprise interesting was the second move: rather than only denying the charges, most of them argued that the best of Greek philosophy had been reaching toward what the church now held, and that Christians were therefore the true heirs of reason rather than its enemies.
relationships.claim: Drew on Greek philosophy, arguing it had been reaching toward Christianity (influenced by Greek philosophy).

relationships.sentence: Justin's argument that the Word was sowing seeds of truth in the philosophers before the incarnation gave the church a way of relating to inherited learning that it has never entirely put down, and that Clement and Origen at Alexandria took much further.
relationships.claim: Justin's idea of seeds of truth in philosophy was taken further by Clement and Origen (led to).

relationships.sentence: This is the Latin counterpart to the Greek apologists of the second century, a generation later and never as coherent a body.
relationships.other: The Greek apologists of the second century
relationships.claim: Latin counterpart (parallel) to the Greek apologists, a generation later.

relationships.sentence: It includes Tertullian, whose Latin apologetic writing opened the tradition and gave it its vocabulary before the other authors continued it.
relationships.claim: Tertullian opened the Latin apologetic tradition (led to).

relationships.sentence: Its clearest link to the later imperial church runs through Lactantius, who wrote his own defense during persecution and then tutored the son of the emperor who ended it.
relationships.other_id_note: Imperial and Juridical Christianity is the nearest census entry; not an exact match.
relationships.claim: Linked to the later imperial church through Lactantius, who tutored Constantine's son.

relationships.sentence: Trinitas, persona, substantia, sacramentum: the technical vocabulary Western Christians still use for the Trinity and the sacraments came substantially off Tertullian's own pen, in the Apology and in the string of treatises that followed it - Against Praxeas arguing that Father and Son are genuinely distinct, the Prescription Against Heretics contending that Scripture belongs to the churches that received it, five long books Against Marcion answering the one rival he judged most dangerous.
relationships.claim: Tertullian argued against Praxeas (modalism).

relationships.sentence: Trinitas, persona, substantia, sacramentum: the technical vocabulary Western Christians still use for the Trinity and the sacraments came substantially off Tertullian's own pen, in the Apology and in the string of treatises that followed it - Against Praxeas arguing that Father and Son are genuinely distinct, the Prescription Against Heretics contending that Scripture belongs to the churches that received it, five long books Against Marcion answering the one rival he judged most dangerous.
relationships.claim: Tertullian argued against Marcion.

relationships.sentence: Trinitas, persona, substantia, sacramentum: the technical vocabulary Western Christians still use for the Trinity and the sacraments came substantially off Tertullian's own pen, in the Apology and in the string of treatises that followed it - Against Praxeas arguing that Father and Son are genuinely distinct, the Prescription Against Heretics contending that Scripture belongs to the churches that received it, five long books Against Marcion answering the one rival he judged most dangerous.
relationships.claim: Tertullian argued that heretics have no standing to cite Scripture.

relationships.sentence: In his later years he grew steadily more rigorist and aligned himself with the New Prophecy out of Phrygia, which is one reason the Latin church quoted him endlessly and never made him a saint.
relationships.claim: Tertullian aligned himself with the New Prophecy (joined).

relationships.sentence: Roughly a generation on and in a very different key, a Roman advocate named Minucius Felix wrote a dialogue set on the beach at Ostia, in which a pagan friend states the case against Christianity - it is a religion of the ignorant, its god was a criminal, Rome's greatness is proof enough that Rome's gods work - and is answered and convinced.
relationships.other: Educated pagan critics (Caecilius in the Octavius)
relationships.other_id_note: Named opponents are pagan critics, not a movement.
relationships.claim: Minucius Felix's dialogue stages and answers the educated pagan case against Christianity (argued against).

relationships.sentence: A century later and in a different register again, an African rhetorician at Sicca called Arnobius wrote seven furious books Against the Heathen - to persuade his own bishop that his conversion was genuine, if Jerome is to be believed - and produced along the way the most detailed account of Roman religious practice that any Christian left, because he had to describe what he was attacking.
relationships.claim: Arnobius argued against pagan religion in seven books Against the Heathen.

relationships.sentence: And at the end of the line stands Lactantius, whom Jerome makes Arnobius' pupil: a professor of Latin rhetoric summoned to Diocletian's new capital at Nicomedia, who lost the post when the persecution began and wrote the Divine Institutes in the middle of it, and who was old by the time it was over, when Constantine brought him to Trier to teach his son.
relationships.other_id_note: State actor, not a movement.
relationships.claim: Lactantius lost his post when Diocletian's persecution began and wrote during it (attacked by state).

relationships.sentence: And at the end of the line stands Lactantius, whom Jerome makes Arnobius' pupil: a professor of Latin rhetoric summoned to Diocletian's new capital at Nicomedia, who lost the post when the persecution began and wrote the Divine Institutes in the middle of it, and who was old by the time it was over, when Constantine brought him to Trier to teach his son.
relationships.other_id_note: Nearest census entry; not an exact match.
relationships.claim: Lactantius later taught Constantine's son (link to the imperial church).

relationships.sentence: A Carthaginian convert named Tertullian had to invent Latin words for the Trinity and the sacraments just to defend his faith, coining terms like trinitas, persona, and substantia.
relationships.claim: Tertullian coined the Latin theological vocabulary this movement used (influenced by).

relationships.sentence: The argument he opened ran a further century, through Minucius Felix's dialogue giving pagan objections their fullest voice, to Lactantius, who wrote his own defense in the middle of persecution and later tutored the emperor's son.
relationships.other_id_note: Nearest census entry; not an exact match.
relationships.claim: Lactantius, the movement's last major figure, later tutored the emperor's son (link to imperial church).

relationships.sentence: Minucius Felix gave the West its model for the apologetic dialogue and preserved, inadvertently, the most complete record of what educated Romans actually said against the church.
relationships.other: Educated Romans who objected to Christianity
relationships.claim: Preserved, through the Octavius, the objections of educated Romans it answered (argued against).

relationships.sentence: And Lactantius' Latin was good enough that the Renaissance called him the Christian Cicero and printed him before it printed most of the Fathers - the Divine Institutes was among the first books off a press in Italy, in 1465.
relationships.claim: Later reception: the Renaissance printed and admired Lactantius.

movements.name: Apocryphal and Pseudepigraphal Literature in Christian Transmission

relationships.sentence: Its natural relation to every other early entry is that they read it.
relationships.other: Every other early Christian movement (they read it)
relationships.claim: Read by all other early movements (influenced them).

relationships.sentence: And a third body is not Christian in origin at all: the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs, the Life of Adam and Eve, the Testament of Abraham are Jewish works that survive because Christian scribes kept copying them, sometimes with Christian passages worked in, after Judaism itself had let them go.
relationships.other: Judaism (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs, Life of Adam and Eve, Testament of Abraham)
relationships.other_id_note: Judaism is a named tradition, not a census movement.
relationships.claim: Some texts are Jewish works that Christian scribes kept copying after Judaism let them go (originated in Judaism).

relationships.sentence: The Dormition narratives that gave the church the Assumption, the tour-of-hell apocalypses that shaped medieval visions of the afterlife, Pseudo-Matthew and its Carolingian abridgement that carried Mary's childhood into the Latin West - these run to the ninth century and beyond.
relationships.other: Carolingian abridgement and the Carolingian Latin West
relationships.other_id_note: Matches by period and region; the link is the text's abridgement, not the reform movement itself.
relationships.claim: Pseudo-Matthew's Carolingian abridgement carried Mary's childhood into the Carolingian West (led to).

relationships.sentence: Some of it carries the apostles into adventures - Andrew among cannibals, Philip at Hierapolis, Thomas in India - in narratives that read like Greek romances and often carry a strongly ascetic charge.
relationships.other: Thomas in India (apocryphal Acts of Thomas)
relationships.other_id_note: The text names only the legend of Thomas in India; it does not tie the Acts to the St Thomas Christians.
relationships.claim: Names the Thomas-in-India legend; possible but unstated link to St Thomas Christians (weak).

relationships.sentence: Some of these works, like the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs, were originally Jewish texts that survive today only because Christian scribes kept copying them long after Judaism itself had let them go.
relationships.other_id_note: Judaism is a named tradition, not a census movement.
relationships.claim: Some works originated as Jewish texts and survived through Christian copying (originated in Judaism).

relationships.sentence: Marian devotion in both East and West rests substantially on the Protevangelium of James: Anna and Joachim, the presentation in the Temple, the ox and the ass, all of it entered the calendar and the iconography from a book the church never accepted as scripture.
relationships.other: Marian devotion in East and West
relationships.claim: Influenced Marian devotion and calendar (led to).

relationships.sentence: The apocryphal Acts supplied medieval art and legend with most of what it knew about the apostles' deaths.
relationships.claim: Influenced medieval art and legend about the apostles (led to).

relationships.sentence: And the Jewish pseudepigrapha in this collection are the reason a large body of Second Temple literature exists at all - preserved, ironically, by the tradition that had parted from the one that produced it.
relationships.other_id_note: Judaism is a named tradition, not a census movement.
relationships.claim: Jewish pseudepigrapha preserved by a Christianity that had parted from Judaism.

relationships.sentence: A contested influence on Desert Monasticism, real at one disputed point and denied as a general continuation; scholarship parent of the Bethlehem Circle
relationships.claim: Contested influence on desert monasticism (influenced).

relationships.sentence: A contested influence on Desert Monasticism, real at one disputed point and denied as a general continuation; scholarship parent of the Bethlehem Circle
relationships.other_id_note: No census entry for the Bethlehem Circle; closest is hieronymian-ascetic-literary.
relationships.claim: Scholarship treats this tradition as parent of the Bethlehem circle (parent of).

relationships.sentence: Origen, who succeeded him, wrote commentaries across most of Scripture and produced the Hexapla, a six-column parallel edition of the Old Testament assembled to see what the Hebrew actually said — before falling out with his bishop and moving his teaching to Caesarea around 231.
relationships.claim: Origen moved his teaching from Alexandria to Caesarea (led to).

relationships.sentence: Nepos, a bishop out in the Egyptian countryside at Arsinoe, wrote a book refuting the allegorists and won real support for a plainer, literal reading — until Dionysius, by then bishop of Alexandria, spent three days in patient public conversation with Nepos's own community and brought them back around.
relationships.other: Nepos and the literalist community at Arsinoe
relationships.other_id_note: Named opponent is a bishop and his community, not a census movement.
relationships.claim: Nepos argued against the allegorical reading of this tradition (argued against).

relationships.sentence: Nepos, a bishop out in the Egyptian countryside at Arsinoe, wrote a book refuting the allegorists and won real support for a plainer, literal reading — until Dionysius, by then bishop of Alexandria, spent three days in patient public conversation with Nepos's own community and brought them back around.
relationships.other_id_note: Named person is a bishop, not a census movement.
relationships.claim: Dionysius won back Nepos's literalist community, opposing that challenge (argued against).

relationships.sentence: Origen's textual scholarship set the standard for taking the original languages seriously; Basil of Caesarea and Gregory of Nazianzus compiled an anthology of his writings, and Ambrose and Jerome read him closely even when they were careful about saying so.
relationships.other: Basil of Caesarea and Gregory of Nazianzus (Cappadocian)
relationships.claim: Cappadocian fathers compiled an anthology of Origen (influenced by).

relationships.sentence: The tradition also fed directly into Egyptian monasticism, giving the desert its intellectual vocabulary.
relationships.claim: Fed directly into desert monasticism (led to).

relationships.sentence: Parent of the Church of the East and the Syriac Orthodox Church; the channel through which Greek philosophy and medicine passed into Arabic and back to Europe.
relationships.other_id_note: Nearest early census entry for the Church of the East.
relationships.claim: Parent of the Church of the East (parent of).

relationships.claim: Channel that passed Greek philosophy and medicine into Arabic and then Europe (led to).

relationships.sentence: They met the Gospel as one continuous story rather than four separate books, in a harmony a Greek-trained convert named Tatian had woven a generation earlier; Aphrahat quoted it and Ephrem preached from it for as long as this Christian tradition lasted.
relationships.other_id_note: Named person does not stand for a census movement.
relationships.claim: The community read Tatian's Gospel harmony as its Gospel text (influenced by Tatian).

relationships.sentence: The community also knew its faith by naming what it was not, answering by name the teachings of the philosopher Bardaisan, of Marcion, and of Mani, all preached in the same cities in the same tongue.
relationships.claim: This community argued against Bardaisan.

relationships.sentence: The community also knew its faith by naming what it was not, answering by name the teachings of the philosopher Bardaisan, of Marcion, and of Mani, all preached in the same cities in the same tongue.

relationships.sentence: Persia's own bishops fought the same question in the open: Papa of Seleucia-Ctesiphon claimed to lead them all, and was contested by his own colleagues in his own lifetime.
relationships.other: Persia's own bishops (Church of the East)
relationships.claim: Internal dispute in the Persian church over leadership (Papa of Seleucia-Ctesiphon).

relationships.sentence: On the Persian side, the persecution already underway since the 340s took bishop Simeon bar Sabbae and his clergy, and left the church's chief seat empty for twenty years, since filling it meant near-certain death.
relationships.other: Persian persecution of the Persian church
relationships.other_id_note: Persian church is the nearest census entry; the persecution was by the Persian state.
relationships.claim: Persian persecution took the Persian church's bishop and clergy (attacked by state).

relationships.sentence: Not until 410, when the Roman bishop Marutha brokered a synod with the favor of Yazdegerd I, the Persian king, did the Persian church finally receive a single settled order—the last thing this tradition's own record has to say.
relationships.claim: Marutha's synod gave the Persian church a single settled order (led to).

relationships.sentence: In 338, Shapur II of Persia besieged Nisibis; Ephrem, the city's own hymnwriter, remembered its deliverance as an act of God worked through ordinary defenders, while a later account added a swarm of gnats to the story.
relationships.other_id_note: State actor, not a movement.
relationships.claim: Persian siege of Nisibis (attack by a state).

relationships.sentence: The Assyrian Church of the East, the Syriac Orthodox Church, and the Eastern Catholic churches in communion with Rome all descend from this tradition, still worship in Syriac, and still sing Ephrem's hymns in their own liturgies.
relationships.claim: Descends from this tradition (led to).

relationships.sentence: Missionaries carried the faith east along the trade routes into Persia and India, and by the seventh century as far as Tang-dynasty China.

relationships.claim: Translators passed Greek philosophy and medicine into the Arabic-speaking world (led to).

relationships.sentence: A separate school of formal theological training later grew up at Nisibis—founded around 490, two generations after this tradition's own record closes—and became one of the ancient world's most important centers of Christian education, distinct from the teaching Jacob and Ephrem had given the same city a century earlier.
relationships.other: School of Nisibis (distinct from the teaching of Jacob and Ephrem)
relationships.other_id_note: School of Nisibis is a later Church of the East institution; match is approximate.
relationships.claim: A separate school at Nisibis, founded later, was distinct from this tradition's teaching (distinct from).

relationships.sentence: Cyprian became bishop of Carthage around 248, went into hiding when the emperor Decius ordered universal sacrifice, and returned to the hardest pastoral problem of the age.
relationships.other_id_note: State actor, not a movement.
relationships.claim: Cyprian fled the Decian persecution (attacked by state).

relationships.sentence: The North African church itself did not survive: the Vandals took the province in the 430s, and the Arab conquest of the seventh century ended Latin Christianity there altogether.

relationships.claim: Opened the tradition the Latin apologists carried on (led to).

relationships.claim: Tertullian argued against Praxeas (modalism).

relationships.sentence: His hymns were popular enough that, a century and a half later, Ephraim the Syrian felt he had to write better ones, even while accusing Bardaisan of a heretical cosmology of primordial beings.
relationships.claim: Ephraim wrote better hymns in response (argued against).

relationships.sentence: Syriac hymnody as a form owes something to both sides of this argument: Bardaisan and his son Harmonius set the pattern, and Ephraim's decision to answer them in the same form gave the Syriac church the madrasha tradition that shaped its worship for centuries.
relationships.claim: Syriac hymnody owes its form to Bardaisan and to Ephraim's answer (influenced).
